thread.title: Federal High Court Orders Remand of Suspected Firearms Smugglers in Lagos
thread.title_full: Federal High Court Orders Remand of Suspected Firearms Smugglers in Lagos

author: GuardianNigeria
title: Federal High Court Orders Remand of Suspected Firearms Smugglers in Lagos
text:
In Lagos, three suspects arrested for transporting pump‑action rifles hidden in a container were remanded by the Federal High Court. The remand, set for 15 days with a follow‑up hearing in September, reflects concerns over the investigation's complexity and the potential jeopardy of releasing the accused. The case underscores the tightening of customs enforcement and judiciary response to illicit arms trafficking.
The Federal High Court in Lagos, presided over by Justice Friday Ogazi, approved a remand request concerning a group of alleged firearms smugglers captured by customs officials in July 2026.
Three individuals were arrested after an investigation uncovered a shipment of pump‑action rifles concealed in a container labeled TEMU 184536/9, which entered Nigerian waters aboard the MV Velika on 8 July. These weapons were reportedly masked within the container's interior, evading standard inspection protocols. The suspects were detained days later, and their cases were brought to court along with a petition filed by the Nigerian Customs Service (NCS).
During the hearing, counsel for the NCS, Mr David Ereh, joined by Mrs Kehinde Bode‑Ayeni, argued that the suspects warranted continued custody pending the completion of a comprehensive inquiry. Their claim rested on several statutory provisions, including Sections 294 and 295 of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act 2015, Section 6 of the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023, pertinent clauses of the 1999 Constitution, and Order 46, Rule 4(d) of the Federal High Court Rules.
The NCS's request was grounded in concerns that the nature of the offenses-illegal importation of arms-would not be adequately investigated within the limited 24 to 48 hour time frame normally required for release on bail. They cited affidavits from a litigation officer, N. Akpan, who detailed the customs operation. According to Akpan, intelligence from the Customs Enforcement Unit linked suspicious activity to the container.
After receiving a directive from the Customs Area Controller, officials monitored the vessel upon its arrival, conducted a physical inspection on 13 July, and uncovered firearms and ammunition within. The arrest of the three suspects followed, and a broader investigation was launched into alleged manipulation of customs documents and forgeries that supposedly facilitated the container's clearance.
The court listened to arguments that the suspects' cooperation could jeopardise the integrity of the probe, as they might provide further information to other alleged conspirators or tamper with evidence. Counsel urged a 15‑day remand in order to secure evidence, track fleeing accomplices, and prevent any interference with ongoing efforts. Justice Ogazi agreed, granting remand and placing the defendants in the custody of the Nigerian Correctional Service for a 15‑day period.
He set a subsequent hearing for 1 September 2026, when investigators will present a progress report or a recommendation for arraignment. The decision underscores the judiciary's role in maintaining public safety when confronting illicit arms trafficking. The case highlights the tightening of customs enforcement and judicial oversight in Nigeria's fight against unlawful gun imports. It illustrates how coordinated efforts between law‑enforcement agencies and the courts can deter the smuggling of dangerous weapons.
The outcomes of the pending investigation and the eventual trial will determine whether the suspects face criminal charges for their role in facilitating the illegal arms movement. The ruling also serves as a reminder that the judicial system may adapt its traditional timelines when serious offenses threaten national security and public health
